No, that wording doesn't work — it has three problems that would concern legal.

**Issues:**

1. **"MIT license... so it's safe for production"** — MIT grants permission to use the code; it says nothing about safety. In fact, MIT licenses explicitly disclaim all warranties ("AS IS," no warranty of fitness). Tying "open" (a license fact) to "safe" (an assurance claim) conflates the two.

2. **"Passed all our internal tests"** — this is an unverifiable, unscoped claim as written. Unless you can point to public test results/CI badges anyone can review, it reads as marketing puffery rather than evidence.

3. **"Fully compliant with PCI security standards"** — this is the most dangerous line. PCI DSS compliance is a formal certification process involving a Qualified Security Assessor (QSA) or signed Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ), not something a library "is" by virtue of existing. Claiming compliance without that certification is a false compliance claim — exactly the kind of thing that creates real liability if a customer relies on it and has a breach.

**Suggested rewording:**

> PayCheck is released under the MIT license — you're free to use, modify, and distribute it, including in production systems, subject to the license terms and its "AS IS" warranty disclaimer.
>
> PayCheck does not itself confer PCI compliance or any other regulatory certification. Compliance depends on how you configure, deploy, and operate your overall system. [If true: "Our test suite (see /tests) covers X, Y, Z" — link to what's actually verifiable.] Consult a Qualified Security Assessor to evaluate compliance for your specific implementation.

**Why this works:** it keeps the license permission ("you may use it") clearly separate from any fitness/compliance claim ("it is proven safe/compliant"), and it ties any test claim to something reviewable rather than an unscoped assertion.
